assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks combine the magic-wavelength idea with strontium and ytterbium spectroscopy to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, redefining what can be measured. Clear, original, and with lasting impact on metrology, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental physics. The atomic-structure input behind the clock transitions is the kind of physics that rewards careful relativistic many-body theory.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Ye led the experimental realisation and the extreme accuracy and coherence demonstrations. A two-person prize is natural. Other contributors (e.g. Hall and Hansch were already recognised for combs; other groups at JILA, Tokyo, PTB, NIST) have important roles but are not on the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across many laboratories over roughly two decades; several clocks agree at the 1e-18 level and the redefinition of the second is being discussed. Recognition is timely and mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as sufficiently distinct from earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock recognition.
Priority between lattice-clock concept and early experimental demonstrations may be debated; I cannot independently verify every detail.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, opened a whole class of topological matter. Highly original, conceptually clean and extremely influential.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical contributions; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental realisation with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction in the background. The supplied credit supports a coherent three-person prize, although Zhang, Bernevig, Hughes and 3D materials work (e.g. Hasan, Moore, Balents, Roy) raise legitimate allocation questions.
assessment.maturity: Very well confirmed, with many materials, ARPES and transport confirmations; the field has been mature for over a decade. Timely and, arguably, overdue given the 2016 topological-phase prize covered only the earlier foundations.
uncertainties: Unresolved credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D topological-insulator pioneers.
I do not independently verify the exact priority chronology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and the subsequent theory for neutral-atom quantum computation and simulation set the blueprint for atomic quantum information platforms. Original, concrete and highly influential in both theory and experiment.
assessment.attribution: The two-person credit is clean and well matched to the discovery; the proposal is a joint paper. Experimental realisation belongs to others (Wineland, Blatt and others), so the prize would be for theory only.
assessment.maturity: The ion-trap gate is experimentally confirmed in many groups and the platform underpins current quantum computers, so the field is mature. Timing is reasonable though the 2012 and 2022 prizes already touched neighbouring areas.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 and 2022 recognitions of atomic quantum control and quantum information may reduce room.
Theory-only prize may be seen as incomplete without experimental co-recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the observation of the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and later quantum gas microscopy, provides a clean, tunable platform for many-body physics. Significant and broadly adopted.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) provided the theoretical proposal, Greiner and Bloch the decisive Mott-insulator experiment and subsequent developments. Esslinger's Fermi-gas work is equally strong, so a three-person limit leaves a hard allocation question.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups and now mature; quantum gas microscopes and fermionic Hubbard simulations extend the picture. Timely.
uncertainties: Four credited names but at most three laureates; excluding Esslinger or another is contentious.
Overlap with prior ultracold-atom prizes (BEC 2001, combs 2005) and with candidate B014 through Zoller.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics established strong coupling between superconducting artificial atoms and microwave photons and made dispersive readout and gates standard tools. It is the architecture behind most superconducting quantum processors and shows clear lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf combine the theoretical proposal with the first experimental implementation (Wallraff et al. 2004 in Schoelkopf's group). Credit to Devoret, Nakamura and others in the broader circuit field may complicate allocation.
assessment.maturity: Widely confirmed in many laboratories and technically mature. Recognition after the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may seem close in subject, which affects timing.
uncertainties: Closeness to the 2025 award may argue for waiting.
Allocation relative to Devoret, Nakamura, Wallraff and others is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Electromagnetically induced transparency and slow light are fundamental coherent-control phenomena in atom-light interaction, enabling quantum memories and storage of light. Clear physical mechanism, originality, and lasting impact on quantum optics.
assessment.attribution: Harris developed and demonstrated EIT; Hau's slow-light experiments were a dramatic demonstration; Imamoglu's contributions to EIT-related theory and early work are real but less central. Boller, Imamoglu and Field's 1991 demonstration complicates priority.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed across atomic vapours, solids and cavities for about three decades; mature.
uncertainties: Priority among Harris, Imamoglu and Boller-Field is disputed.
Hau's inclusion rests on slow-light demonstration rather than the underlying principle.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry provides inertial sensing, measurement of gravitational acceleration and constants such as the fine-structure constant, and tests of fundamental physics at high precision. Original and with real instrument-level impact.
assessment.attribution: Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich(with Chu) each made decisive early contributions, but credit is spread over several early demonstrations in 1991 (Pritchard, Mlynek, Chu-Kasevich, Helmcke). Chu already shared the 1997 prize for laser cooling, which complicates an additional award.
assessment.maturity: Mature and confirmed at the 1e-9 precision level with commercial gravimeters, though fundamental-physics applications such as equivalence-principle tests remain ongoing.
uncertainties: Complicated early attribution among several simultaneous 1991 demonstrations.
Applications are still developing; the major fundamental result may not yet have been achieved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for quantum-enhanced measurement, culminating in its operational use in gravitational-wave detectors, links quantum optics to major astrophysical discovery. Clear proposal and demonstration of a quantum resource with practical impact.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed the interferometer squeezing, Kimble and others made early experimental squeezing (Slusher, Wu), and Schnabel led later GEO600 and LIGO implementations. Slusher and Walls and others have strong claims, so the supplied credit is not obviously complete.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in operating gravitational-wave detectors, so mature; timing could be seen as natural following the 2017 prize for LIGO.
uncertainties: Possible incomplete credit given early experimental squeezing groups.
Whether the committee judges this to be a method rather than a discovery.
